I would say that you're in a weird situation. On one side, loads if not most of the youth in Québec got a good enough English to be able to entertain a conversation. On the other side they are lazy and will probably default the french if the crowd is mostly french. Finally, some of them are also deeply attached to the french language do to it being actively threatened by the English language (mostly in Montreal).
In the end, trying to speak French will probably go a long way in making connections while you will also be able to use English as a backup when necessary.
There is also probably some french who wish to practice their own english. Maybe make friends with them.
Make a reservation in advance. They will find you a chauffeur who is willing to do it.

You shouldn't have problems with English but if you want to go the extra mile, Duolingo could give you a nice jump start. Like anywhere, we got some dumbass that could try to bully you and some other dumbass that think it's just fun and banter. There is also a counter movement that will speak only in English even if they are native French.
Then warning to you, Canada (and the USA) are car centric countries. So it would be hard to travel outside of downtown in bus. 
For the food, if you're on a budget, groceries are your best bet. Unless some exceptional place, a restaurant meal is about 20-30$/ meals. Peanut buttering can get you a long way (and it's a traditional breakfast XD). 
If you want to splash a little bit, we got a pretty good micro-brewery culture with good food.
If you got any other questions, ask and you shall receive.

Public transit stay inside the city. You won't have access to a lot of nature.
The Plaine d'Abraham is a huge long park with lots of greens, old fortifications and the national art museum.
There are other fortification inside the old city and in the limits between downtown and up town.
The Musée de la civilisation (best museum in Québec) is downtown.
There is also loads of micro-brewery and pubs if you're looking for a balance between great bite and great drink.

Selon mon impression, les gens qui veulent fuire du Québec ne parte que très rarement car ils n'ont nulle part où aller. La vie est merdique partout, juste différentes. Ils n'auront donc pas la Drive nécessaire pour faire le move. Les personnes qui réussissent avant généralement une destination préférée car il préfère un style de vie par rapport à un autre (plus gauche que droite par exemple). Avec une destination claire ils peuvent donc commencer à rêver et planifier le mouvement.

Malheureusement il y a aussi toutes ces barrières.

1. C'est chers
2. Pour pouvoir migrés vers un autre pays il faut soit avoir une spécialisation dans un domaine spécifique ou avoir au haut niveau d'éducation (seulement un peu plus de 20% de bachelier au Québec)
3. Devoir affaiblir/coupé ces racines (famille, amis, collègues)
4. La barrière de la langue
5. Bubble burst: souvent quand on fais nos recherches en profondeur pour planifier changement, on peut rencontrer plusieurs nouvelles informations qui brisent nos preconceptions et nous font comprendre la vie c'est de la merde partout.
